job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Lena Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior brand analyst at a yoghurt and dessert company near Lyon. I track how our products sell, test ad ideas and write the weekly market summary for the brand manager. I studied marketing and business, passed, no internships, and started in August. I live in a small flat with my boyfriend Hugo, who teaches. I use AI all day for first drafts, charts and quick research, and in the evening I run a little newsletter about food trends, which has about nine hundred subscribers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's okay, it was never going to be a miracle. I'd tell friends it's like spell-check for everything, helpful, and I'd keep using it. Online I'd write one calm post and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit disappointed, because I've built my week around it and I like being ahead. But my job is secure either way, because the brand team needs people who understand shoppers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job, keep the newsletter going and try to grow it past a thousand readers. I'd save 300 a month, and use the weekends to take a short course in consumer research.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's an easy world to live in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Setting AI aside, what about the next two years do you actually lose sleep over, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The only thing that nags me is rent. Lyon is pricey, and Hugo's teaching salary is modest. We have my savings of about nine thousand, but I'd love a bit more padding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If money got tight or work got harder anyway, who or what would you point to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really anyone. Prices went up everywhere, and wages haven't followed. Politicians on both sides say they'll fix it and don't, but that's the story of my whole life.

I'd write one calm post online and leave it there.
think: I'd be a bit **disappointed**, since I've built my week around AI.
The brand team still needs people who understand **shoppers**.
do: Keep the **newsletter** going and aim for a thousand readers.
Save **300 a month** and take a short course in consumer research.
feel: **Calm**; it's an easy world to live in.

fieldNote: Her **adaptive** habits make a quiet world feel slightly flat.

steps.text: Grow the food newsletter past a thousand readers

Take a short course in consumer research

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what's already happening, just faster. I'd tell the team we should be the first to use it properly, and I'd show colleagues the prompts that work. Online I'd write about how marketing jobs are changing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a bit scary because my job is thinking and writing, which is the target. The weekly summary, the ad copy and the charts are all things a good tool does. What's left for me is taste and judgement, and I don't know how many juniors that supports.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lean harder into strategy: talk to shoppers, run small tests, tell the brand manager what to try. I'd grow the newsletter into something with paid sponsors. I'd also learn the basics of coding, so I can build my own tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but it's kind of a game. I like games.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of your own week would software take over first, and would anyone notice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The weekly market summary. It takes me four hours now and a tool could do it in ten minutes. My manager would notice because I'd have time to ask for more important projects, or because she'd ask why we need me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask your employer to do, if you could ask for anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a say in how it's brought in, and training for the whole team, not just me. And I'd want it understood that the time saved goes into better work, not fewer people.

say: I'd say it's already happening, just **faster**, and show colleagues prompts that work.
I'd write about how marketing jobs are changing.
think: My job is **thinking and writing**, which is the target.
What's left is **taste and judgement**, and I don't know how many juniors that supports.
do: Shift to **strategy**: talk to shoppers, run small tests and advise the brand manager.
Grow the newsletter into one with **paid sponsors**.
feel: **Uneasy**, but it feels a bit like a game.
S1.quote: The weekly market summary. It takes me four hours now and a tool could do it in ten minutes.
fieldNote: Honest that the **summary** she writes weekly is the first task to go.
Plans to move to taste, strategy and tests.
Uses the newsletter as a **hedge** against the day-job shrinking.

steps.text: Run small consumer tests and present results to the brand manager

Teach colleagues the prompts that work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too much, and that we should help whoever gets caught out. I'd be quick to say, don't panic but don't wait either. I'd post a thread about it, and I'd probably get a lot of angry replies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm rattled. Two years is no time to turn myself into anything senior. If the tool does all the thinking, my degree and my first job count for little. My edge is that I already live with the tools, but so does everyone else my age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd throw myself at the newsletter and a small online business, perhaps a food consultancy for small producers using the tools. I'd put savings toward twelve months of living costs, about thirteen thousand. Hugo and I would stop talking about moving to a bigger flat. And I'd ask my boss if I can be the one who trains the team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd get on with something. Sitting still would be worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is short. What do you do in the first month after you hear it's real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd write down every skill I have that isn't just typing, like talking to shoppers and spotting a trend. Then I'd tell three small producers I know that I can help them. If someone pays, I've got a business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you say to your family, and what do you leave out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Hugo everything and we'd make a budget together. My parents get the short version, because my dad would worry loudly. I'd leave out how much I'm worried I might not find another job.

say: I'd say **don't panic** but don't wait either, and post a thread about it.
I'd say we should help whoever gets caught out.
think: Two years is no time to turn myself into anything **senior**, and my degree would count for little.
Everyone my age also **lives with the tools**.
do: Build a small **food consultancy** for local producers and grow the newsletter.
Save toward **twelve months** of living costs and offer to train the team.
feel: **Anxious**, but I'd get on with something; sitting still is worse.
S2.quote: My edge is that I already live with the tools, but so does everyone else my age.
fieldNote: Anxious but **action-first**: she begins with her own skills.
Treats the newsletter as the seed of a business.
Keeps her worst fears from her **dad** and partner's worry.

steps.text: Pitch a food consultancy to three small producers
Save toward twelve months of living costs
Offer to train my team on the AI tools
Make a shared budget with Hugo

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to do something clever, so let's not waste it. I'd tell people to start small things now, so they've got options. I'd say it in the newsletter and to the brand team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I feel pretty good. In five years I could have a real business, or a good senior role, or both. I'd be twenty-seven, with savings and a name in food trends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one I'd grow the newsletter to three thousand and add sponsors, move into a strategy role in the company, and learn a bit of data science. I'd save about 500 a month, and start putting a bit into index funds. I'd also keep up with the AI tools as they change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited. It's the world where being nosy about new things pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years instead of two. What does that extra time change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years I'd test two or three small business ideas. If one works, I could drop my day job. With two years I'd only have time for one attempt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does your money go during those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly savings and funds. A little into the newsletter, maybe paying a designer. I'd also set up a cushion for Hugo and me in case either of us needs to take a pause.

say: I'd say five years is long enough to do something **clever**, so let's not waste it.
I'd tell people to start **small things** now.
think: I feel pretty good: in five years I could have a real **business** or a senior role.
I'd be twenty-seven with savings and a **name** in food trends.
do: Grow the newsletter to **three thousand** readers and add sponsors.
Save **500 a month**, start index funds and move into strategy.
feel: **Calm** and a bit excited; being nosy about new things pays.
S3.quote: With five years I'd test two or three small business ideas. If one works, I could drop my day job.
fieldNote: Five years converts **curiosity** into a portfolio of small bets.
Index funds begin as a second cushion.
She takes **risk** more easily because savings and a partner's income exist.

steps.text: Grow the newsletter to three thousand readers with sponsors
Move into a strategy role at the company
Put 500 a month into savings and index funds

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the best-case timing: enough time to do it well. I'd say companies should use these ten years to retrain people properly, and governments should work out taxes and safety nets. But I'd also say, don't sit and wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm optimistic. At thirty-two I could be running a brand, or my own small company. The danger is complacency, because everyone gets used to the slow ramp.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the day job, build the newsletter and a few side projects, and invest steadily. Maybe a master's in a year or two if it helps. I'd start a family with Hugo around thirty, knowing the money's there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I'd sleep fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long runway. What can you do with that time that you couldn't with two or five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I could build something that's mine, a brand or a media business, with people working for me. With two years I'd just be reacting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you still want to be in this kind of work by then, or something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not the same one. I'd want to run things, not write the weekly summary. Whoever the machine can't replace is the person who knows what people actually want.

say: I'd say it's the **best-case timing**, enough time to do it well.
I'd say companies should retrain people properly, and nobody should sit and wait.
think: I'm optimistic: at thirty-two I could be running a **brand** or my own company.
The danger is **complacency**, because everyone gets used to the slow ramp.
do: Keep the day job, build the newsletter and **invest steadily**.
Maybe do a master's and start a **family** with Hugo around thirty.
S4.quote: With ten years I could build something that's mine, a brand or a media business, with people working for me.
fieldNote: Ten years: her ambition shifts from **keeping** a job to building a company.
Family plans appear for the first time.

steps.text: Build the newsletter into a small media business
Invest part of every pay cheque steadily
Plan a family with Hugo around thirty
Keep using the newest AI tools at work

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, but only mildly, because I'd rather be scrambling with the tools than without them. What would help is a savings cushion, an employer who tells the truth and enough time to try a business.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people my age are often told we're glued to our phones. Actually we're the ones who have to work out how to live with all this.

headlineQuote: We're the ones who have to work out how to live with all this.
portrait: Lena is 22, a **junior brand analyst** at a dessert company near Lyon, in the job since August.
She uses **AI all day**, teaches colleagues the prompts that work, and runs a newsletter with about nine hundred readers.
A pragmatic centrist, she blames no side in particular and treats rent and prices as everyone's problem.
With nine thousand saved, a partner's salary and plenty of openings, she stays **calm** or uneasy, anxious only at two years.
Given time she plans side businesses, index funds, a family and eventually a company of her own.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI world worries her most, but only mildly, since she'd rather scramble with the tools.
whatWouldHelp: She wants a **savings cushion**, an honest employer and enough time to try a business.
